title: Design a Load Balancer
summary: Keep traffic moving through healthy servers: put an L4 ECMP tier and L7 proxy fleet behind one VIP, choose a balancing algorithm, combine active and passive health checks, drain connections, handle TLS and roll out config safely.
body:
## Practice first

Design the load balancer that sits in front of a company's web and API fleet: it accepts all inbound HTTPS traffic on a few public IP addresses, terminates TLS, routes requests by host and path to the right backend pool, and keeps sending traffic only to healthy servers while those servers are deployed, scaled and replaced. Assume you are building the load balancer itself, not configuring a managed one.

Start with a 10-minute sketch: what one load balancer does, why one machine is not enough, how many machines share one public IP, and what happens to in-flight requests when a backend leaves. Then compare your design.

## Functional requirements

Core (users should be able to):

1. **Clients** reach services through a stable hostname/IP; their requests are forwarded to a healthy backend in the right pool and the response is returned.
2. **Service owners** define routing rules (host, path prefix, header match → backend pool), weights for canaries, and health check settings, and changes apply within seconds.
3. **Operators** add, drain and remove backends (and load balancer nodes) without dropping in-flight requests.

Out of scope: global traffic management between regions (DNS/GSLB, covered briefly at the end), a web application firewall, and DDoS scrubbing beyond basic SYN-flood protection.

## Non-functional requirements

- **Scale:** 500k requests/s at peak, 2 million concurrent client connections (many idle keep-alives and WebSockets), 20 Gbps.
- **Latency:** the load balancer adds under 1 ms at p99 for an established connection; new TLS handshakes are dominated by network round trips.
- **Availability:** 99.99% or better, higher than any service behind it, because everything depends on it. No single node, rack or zone failure may drop the virtual IP.
- **Consistency of routing state:** config may be eventually consistent across nodes for a few seconds, but a bad config must never reach the whole fleet at once.
- **Correctness under change:** a node or backend leaving must not reset established connections more than necessary.

## Back-of-the-envelope

- **TLS handshakes decide the L7 fleet size.** Full handshakes cost much more CPU than proxying established traffic. Assume 20% of requests arrive on new connections → 100k handshakes/s. With ECDSA P-256 certificates, a modern core manages on the order of several thousand full handshakes per second (RSA-2048 signing is several times slower). Budgeting ~5k per core and 50% headroom, that is ~40 cores just for handshakes, so we **use ECDSA certificates, TLS session resumption and long keep-alives**, which cut full handshakes sharply.
- **Proxy throughput:** a well-tuned L7 proxy instance on 16 cores handles very roughly 30–60k HTTPS requests/s. 500k/s ÷ 40k ≈ 13 nodes; with N+2 per zone across three zones, about **18 L7 nodes**.
- **Connection memory:** 2M connections × ~20–50 KB of buffers and TLS state ≈ 40–100 GB across the fleet, a few GB per node: fine, but it means idle-connection timeouts matter.
- **One public IP, many nodes:** 20 Gbps exceeds a single 10/25 Gbps NIC with headroom, so a **layer-4 tier that spreads one VIP across many nodes** is required, not optional.

## Core entities

- **Listener:** VIP, port, protocol, TLS certificates (by SNI).
- **Route:** match (host, path prefix, headers) → backend pool with weights.
- **Backend pool:** set of endpoints, balancing algorithm, health check spec, outlier detection settings.
- **Endpoint:** IP:port, zone, health state, weight, draining flag.
- **Config snapshot:** a versioned bundle of all the above, the unit of rollout.

## API

The data plane speaks HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSockets to clients. The control plane has a management API:

```http
PUT /v1/pools/checkout
{ "algorithm": "least_request", "healthCheck": { "path": "/healthz", "intervalMs": 2000,
  "unhealthyThreshold": 3, "healthyThreshold": 2 }, "outlierDetection": { "consecutive5xx": 5 } }

PUT /v1/routes/shop
{ "host": "shop.example.com",
  "rules": [ { "pathPrefix": "/api/checkout", "pool": "checkout", "weight": 95 },
             { "pathPrefix": "/api/checkout", "pool": "checkout-canary", "weight": 5 } ] }

POST /v1/pools/checkout/endpoints/10.0.4.17:8080:drain
{ "timeoutSeconds": 60 }
202 Accepted
```

Every write produces a new config version; `GET /v1/config/versions?cursor=...` lists them for audit and rollback. Management calls require operator auth and are audited.

## High-level design

**Requirement 1, forward traffic.** Two tiers. A **layer-4 tier** owns the public VIPs: routers spread packets across L4 nodes with ECMP, and each L4 node picks an L7 node per connection by hashing the 5-tuple. The **layer-7 tier** terminates TLS, parses HTTP, matches routes and proxies to backends over pooled, keep-alive connections.

**Requirement 2, configure.** A control plane validates changes, stores versioned snapshots and pushes them to L7 nodes over a streaming API (Envoy's xDS is a common model); nodes apply them without restarting.

**Requirement 3, change membership.** Backends register via service discovery; health checks and draining decide when traffic moves.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Clients"] --> DNS["DNS: shop.example.com"]
    DNS --> RT["Edge routers (ECMP, anycast VIP)"]
    RT --> L4A["L4 node"]
    RT --> L4B["L4 node"]
    L4A --> L7A["L7 proxy (TLS, routing)"]
    L4B --> L7B["L7 proxy (TLS, routing)"]
    L7A --> P1["Pool: checkout"]
    L7B --> P2["Pool: catalog"]
    CP["Control plane"] -.->|"versioned config"| L7A
    CP -.-> L7B
    SD[("Service discovery")] -.-> CP
```

Walk a request: `shop.example.com` resolves to a VIP. Routers advertise that VIP and spread flows across L4 nodes using ECMP. The L4 node hashes the connection's 5-tuple to choose an L7 node and forwards packets (often encapsulated, with direct server return so responses skip the L4 tier). The L7 node completes the TLS handshake using the certificate selected by SNI, reads `POST /api/checkout`, matches the route, picks a healthy endpoint with least-request balancing, and sends the request over an existing upstream connection. It adds `X-Forwarded-For` and a request ID, streams the response back, and records latency and status for that endpoint.

## Deep dives

### 1. L4 vs L7, and why both (scale and availability)

| | Layer 4 | Layer 7 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sees | IPs, ports, TCP/UDP | HTTP method, host, path, headers |
| Decision unit | Connection (flow) | Request |
| Cost | Very cheap, kernel/XDP fast path | TLS + parsing, much more CPU |
| Can do | Spread flows, survive node loss | Path routing, retries, canaries, auth, HTTP/2 multiplexing |

**Bad:** one big L7 box with a floating IP; a failover pair (VRRP active/passive) works for small sites but caps throughput at one machine and wastes the passive node.

**Good:** DNS round robin across several L7 nodes; but clients cache DNS, so a dead node keeps receiving traffic for the TTL and beyond.

**Great:** ECMP plus a stateless-ish L4 tier in front of an L7 fleet. Routers hash flows to L4 nodes; L4 nodes use **consistent hashing** (Google's Maglev hashing is the classic example) to pick L7 nodes and keep a small connection table, so when an L4 node is added or removed, existing flows still map to the same L7 node and are not reset. The same VIP is announced from several sites with **anycast** when you go multi-region.

### 2. Picking a backend (latency)

- **Round robin:** fine when requests and servers are uniform. Breaks with mixed request costs.
- **Least connections / least outstanding requests:** adapts to slow servers, but a global "least" needs global state.
- **Power of two choices (P2C):** each L7 node picks two random healthy endpoints and sends to the one with fewer outstanding requests from that node. Near-optimal balance with no coordination; the default in several modern proxies.
- **Latency-weighted (EWMA):** penalise endpoints whose recent latency rises; good for heterogeneous hardware.
- **Consistent hashing on a key (user ID, cookie):** for cache affinity or sticky sessions. Use bounded-load consistent hashing so a hot key cannot overload one server; prefer making services stateless over relying on stickiness.

Recommendation: P2C least-request by default, ring hash only for pools that need affinity, and **slow start** (ramping weight over 30–60 s) for new endpoints with cold caches or JITs.

### 3. Health checks that do not cause outages (availability)

**Bad: TCP-connect health checks only.** A process that accepts connections but returns 500s, or a deadlocked app, stays "healthy".

**Good: active HTTP checks** to `/healthz` every 2 s; mark unhealthy after 3 failures and healthy after 2 successes (hysteresis prevents flapping). The endpoint should check the process's own ability to serve, not every downstream dependency; otherwise one database blip marks the whole pool unhealthy at once.

**Great: active + passive.** Passive **outlier detection** ejects an endpoint that returns 5 consecutive 5xx or times out on live traffic, for a back-off period that grows on repeated ejection, capped at a maximum ejection percentage. A **panic threshold** says: if more than, say, 50% of a pool looks unhealthy, assume the health signal is wrong and spread traffic across all endpoints rather than crushing the few "healthy" ones.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    H["Healthy"] -->|"3 failed checks or 5 consecutive 5xx"| U["Ejected"]
    U -->|"2 passed checks after back-off"| SS["Slow start"]
    SS -->|"weight ramps up over 60 s"| H
    H -->|"operator drain"| D["Draining"]
    D -->|"connections closed or timeout"| R["Removed"]
```

Bring a recovering endpoint back gradually rather than giving it a full share of traffic at once. Keep draining separate: operators or deployments request it; a failure does not.

### 4. Removing backends and LB nodes gracefully (correctness under change)

A deployment may replace backends every few minutes. If you stop a process while it is serving requests, those requests can become 502s. Give them a chance to finish first.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant O as Deployer
    participant CP as Control plane
    participant L7 as L7 proxies
    participant B as Backend 10.0.4.17
    O->>CP: drain 10.0.4.17 (60 s)
    CP->>L7: config v42: endpoint draining
    L7->>L7: stop new requests to B
    L7->>B: finish in-flight requests
    Note over L7,B: HTTP/1.1 Connection: close, HTTP/2 GOAWAY
    L7-->>CP: active requests on B = 0
    CP-->>O: drained
    O->>B: SIGTERM
```

Draining stops new requests, lets in-flight ones finish up to a timeout, and closes idle upstream connections cleanly. The backend should also handle SIGTERM by failing its readiness check and finishing work. The same idea applies to L7 nodes: withdraw the node from the L4 tier's table, let long-lived connections finish (or send GOAWAY so HTTP/2 clients reconnect elsewhere), and only then stop it. WebSockets may need a longer drain window or an application-level reconnect.

### 5. TLS and config rollout (blast radius)

**TLS termination at L7** lets the proxy route on HTTP and reuse upstream connections. Keep private keys in a secrets manager or HSM-backed service, load certificates by SNI, automate renewal (ACME) with expiry alerts, and re-encrypt to backends (mTLS) if the internal network is not trusted. If a team needs end-to-end TLS without the LB seeing plaintext, offer **TLS passthrough** at L4 and accept losing path routing for that listener.

**Config rollout** is the most common cause of load balancer outages. The control plane validates each snapshot (schema, references to existing pools, no route shadowing an existing route unexpectedly), pushes it to one canary node per zone, watches error rates for a few minutes, then rolls out progressively. Nodes keep the last known good config if the control plane is unreachable: the data plane must **fail static**, never empty. Every snapshot is versioned, so rollback is one push.

**Across regions**, DNS-based global load balancing (latency- or geo-based answers with health checks and short TTLs) or anycast VIPs steer clients to the nearest healthy region; each region runs the design above.

## What interviewers look for

- **Mid-level:** explains L4 vs L7, a sensible algorithm, active health checks, TLS termination and that the LB itself needs redundancy.
- **Senior:** designs the two-tier VIP architecture (ECMP, consistent hashing, connection tracking), passive outlier detection with panic thresholds, connection draining and slow start, and sizes the fleet from handshake costs.
- **Staff:** treats config as the biggest risk (validation, canarying, fail-static data plane), separates control and data planes cleanly, reasons about multi-region steering and blast radius, and defines the SLOs and signals (per-endpoint error rates, ejection counts, drain times).

## Common mistakes

- A single LB, or an active/passive pair, presented as highly available at 20 Gbps.
- Health checks that depend on downstream services, so one dependency outage ejects every backend.
- No hysteresis or slow start, causing flapping and thundering herds on recovery.
- Removing backends without draining, then blaming the deploy for 502s.
- Sticky sessions as the default instead of stateless services.
- Pushing config to every node at once with no validation or rollback.

## Self-review checklist

- [ ] One VIP is served by many nodes, and losing one node does not reset most flows.
- [ ] The L7 fleet is sized from a stated per-node capacity and TLS handshake cost.
- [ ] The balancing algorithm handles uneven request costs.
- [ ] Health checking combines active probes, passive ejection and a panic threshold.
- [ ] Draining and slow start exist for both backends and LB nodes.
- [ ] Config changes are validated, canaried, versioned and fail static.
- [ ] TLS keys and certificate renewal have an owner and alerts.

## Further reading

- [Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer (NSDI 2016)](https://research.google/pubs/maglev-a-fast-and-reliable-software-network-load-balancer/)
- [Envoy: load balancing overview](https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/latest/intro/arch_overview/upstream/load_balancing/overview)
- [HAProxy documentation](https://docs.haproxy.org/)
keyTakeaways: Put many nodes behind one VIP using ECMP and a consistent-hashing L4 tier. An active/passive pair still limits throughput to one machine.
Size the L7 fleet around TLS handshake cost. ECDSA certificates, session resumption and keep-alives reduce that work.
Power-of-two-choices least-request balances work without global state. Save bounded-load hashing for pools that actually need affinity.
Health is more than a probe: combine active checks, passive outlier ejection, hysteresis, slow start and a panic threshold.
Drain connections before removing nodes. Treat config rollout as the main outage risk: validate it, try canaries, keep versions and fail static.
